Through sorbent optimization and process design improvements, it is estimated that the cost of capture was reduced from $349/tCO to $241/tCO . The TEA projects further reductions to 2 2 $165/tCO through enhancements in CO adsorption rate and sorbent capacity and reducing manufacturing 2 2 and scale up risks. A life cycle analysis was conducted on the same 100,000 TPY facility and confirmed that the facility’s electricity demand drives its greenhouse gas impact. It was determined that electricity supplied through the current grid mix would result in net-positive CO emissions and that achieving net- 2 negative emissions is only possible by powering the DAC system with renewable electricity or fossil fuel sources equipped with carbon capture and sequestration. Project Objective and Accomplishments The project objective was to lower the cost of CO removal from air by developing a high capacity direct 2 air capture (DAC) sorbent and a novel, low pressure drop, structured sorbent assembly capable of direct, joule-heated regeneration, that can utilize commercially available manufacturing infrastructure for rapid scale-up. Key targets for the sorbent development included: 1. High CO loading capacity (>5 wt% CO ) – lower operating cost for sorbent regeneration and 2 2 capital cost by reducing the size of the DAC contactor/number of DAC module 2. High Stability (<5% capacity fade over 100 adsorption-regeneration cycles) – lower operating costs for sorbent make-up 3. High CO adsorption rate (>0.03 gmolCO /gSorbent-min) – lower capital cost by reducing 2 2 Key targets for the structured sorbent development include: 1. Low cost of structured sorbent manufacturing 2. High DAC sorbent loading capacity on structured substrate – lower operating cost for sorbent regeneration and lower capital cost by reducing size of DAC contactor/number of modules 3. Capable of direct Joule-heated sorbent regeneration – reduce operating costs by efficient use of available electricity 4. Utilize existing manufacturing infrastructure for rapid scale-up Over the course of this project, the sorbent and structured sorbent assembly were optimized and developed, respectively, to achieve the performance targets discussed above. The synthesis of the optimized sorbent was then scaled to produce 50 kg of sorbent, which was sent to a commercial partner to manufacture the structured sorbent filters. In addition, a bench scale unit was designed and fabricated, which was used to test the structured sorbent filter with Joule-heated regeneration. The structured sorbent filter was then tested at the bench scale in three configurations to ultimately maximize sorbent capacity in stability. A techno-economic analysis of a 100,000 TPY DAC facility employing Susteon’s structured sorbent filter technology found that marginal improvements in the sorbent performance resulted in a substantial reduction in the cost of CO capture.
